paper.title: Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Perturbations

project.title: Does AI Still See Clearly in Fog, Blur and Noise?
project.question: How much does a small image classifier trained on clean CIFAR-10 photos lose accuracy on blurred, noisy and foggy versions from CIFAR-10-C, which corruptions hurt most, and can a simple training augmentation reduce the drop?
project.hypothesis: Accuracy will fall as corruption severity rises, noise and blur will hurt more than mild brightness changes, and training with simple augmentations will shrink the drop on some corruptions but not all.
data: CIFAR-10-C from Zenodo (corrupted test images, 5 severities)
risks: The CIFAR-10-C download is several gigabytes; download it once in Colab and load only the corruptions you need.
Training on a CPU is slow; use a free GPU runtime and a small network.
Results on small 32x32 images may not carry over to large real-world photos; say so in your limitations.

milestones.title: Look at clean and corrupted images
milestones.deliverable: Notebook showing the same test images clean and under several corruptions at severities 1 and 5, with a label check

stuck.label: I don't understand how the corrupted files are organized
hints: Read the dataset description on the download page. What does each file contain, and how are the severity levels arranged inside it?

Each corruption is stored as one numpy array file holding the test images at every severity level, one block after another, with one shared label file. Slicing the array by position gives you a single severity.

Skeleton:
```python
import numpy as np
x = np.load(___)  # one corruption file
y = np.load(___)  # labels file
sev = ___  # severity from 1 to 5
x_s = x[(sev - 1) * 10000 : sev * 10000]
```

stuck.label: My images look wrong when I plot them
hints: Print the shape and data type of one image. Is the color channel first or last?
matplotlib expects images as height × width × channels, with values from 0 to 255 as integers or 0 to 1 as floats. PyTorch tensors usually put channels first, so you may need to move that axis.
Analogous example: a photo saved as rows of blue, then green, then red needs reordering before a viewer that expects red first can show it correctly. Check your axis order the same way.

stuck.label: I'm not sure the labels match the images
hints: Pick five images and their labels at random. Do the pictures look like the class names?
Corrupted test sets reuse the order of the clean test set, so image i at any severity should have the same label as clean test image i. A quick visual check catches slicing mistakes early.

Skeleton:
```python
classes = [___]  # the ten CIFAR-10 class names
for i in np.random.choice(10000, 5):
    plt.imshow(x_s[i]); plt.title(classes[y[___]]); plt.show()
```

milestones.title: Train a baseline classifier
milestones.deliverable: Small CNN trained on clean CIFAR-10 with its clean test accuracy and training curves

stuck.label: My model trains very slowly
hints: Is your notebook actually using a GPU? How can you check which device PyTorch is running on?
Free cloud notebooks offer a GPU runtime that must be switched on. Moving both the model and each batch to the GPU device makes training much faster than a CPU.

Skeleton:
```python
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = model.to(___)
for xb, yb in loader:
    xb, yb = xb.to(___), yb.to(___)
```

stuck.label: My accuracy stays low
hints: Plot training loss and accuracy for each epoch. Are they improving at all, and is the training accuracy much higher than the test accuracy?
Low accuracy can come from too few epochs, a learning rate that is too high or too low, unnormalized inputs, or a network that is too small. Changing one thing at a time shows which one matters.
Analogous example: when a recipe fails, a cook changes the oven temperature or the baking time, not both at once. Keep a small table of each change and its effect on validation accuracy.

stuck.label: I don't know when to stop training
hints: What happens to the validation accuracy in the last few epochs compared with the training accuracy?
If training accuracy keeps rising while validation accuracy flattens or falls, the model is starting to overfit. Many projects stop at the epoch with the best validation accuracy and save that model.

Skeleton:
```python
best = 0
for epoch in range(___):
    train_one_epoch(); acc = evaluate(___)
    if acc > best: best = acc; torch.save(model.state_dict(), ___)
```

milestones.title: Measure the robustness gap
milestones.deliverable: Table and plot of accuracy for at least five corruptions across severities, compared with clean accuracy

stuck.label: I don't know how to compare corruptions fairly
hints: Are you testing every corruption on the same images, with the same model and the same preprocessing?

A fair comparison keeps the model, the images and the preprocessing fixed and changes only the corruption and its severity. The paper also reports errors relative to a baseline model so corruptions of different difficulty can be compared.
Table skeleton for your notebook: corruption | severity 1 | severity 3 | severity 5 | clean. Fill one row per corruption with accuracy from the same saved model.

stuck.label: My results change every time I run
hints: Which parts of your code use randomness, and did you fix a seed for them?
Weight initialization, shuffling and augmentation all use random numbers. Fixing seeds makes runs repeatable, and repeating with a few different seeds shows how much results naturally vary.

Skeleton:
```python
import random
for s in [___, ___, ___]:
    random.seed(s); np.random.seed(s); torch.manual_seed(s)
    # train, evaluate, store the accuracy for seed s
```

stuck.label: I'm not sure how to show the results
hints: What should a reader see first: which corruption is hardest, or how accuracy changes with severity?
A line plot with severity on the x-axis and accuracy on the y-axis, one line per corruption, shows both patterns at once. A dashed line for clean accuracy gives a reference.

Skeleton:
```python
for name, accs in results.items():
    plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], accs, label=name)
plt.axhline(___, linestyle="--", label="clean")
plt.legend(); plt.show()
```

milestones.title: Try an augmentation
milestones.deliverable: Second model trained with one augmentation and a side-by-side comparison with the baseline

stuck.label: I don't know which augmentation to try
hints: Which corruptions hurt your baseline most? What kind of training change might prepare a model for those?

Data augmentation randomly changes training images, for example by flipping, cropping, adding noise or blurring, so the model learns to ignore those changes. torchvision provides many transforms you can chain together.

Skeleton:
```python
from torchvision import transforms as T
train_tf = T.Compose([T.RandomHorizontalFlip(), ___, T.ToTensor()])
```

stuck.label: Augmentation made clean accuracy drop
hints: Compare both models on clean and corrupted images together. Did the drop on clean images come with a gain somewhere else?
Robustness methods often trade a little clean accuracy for better accuracy under corruption. Reporting both numbers side by side lets readers judge the trade-off.
Analogous example: winter tires grip worse on dry roads but much better on snow. Describe your augmentation's trade-off in the same way, with your own measurements.

stuck.label: I'm afraid I tested on corruptions I trained with
hints: List the transforms you used in training and the corruptions you tested. Do any of them overlap?
If you train with a transform that matches a test corruption, the gain on that corruption says less about general robustness. Report overlapping and non-overlapping corruptions separately.
Table skeleton: corruption | seen in training? | baseline accuracy | augmented accuracy. Discuss the 'not seen' rows first.

milestones.title: Write the report
milestones.deliverable: 4-page report: question, method, results, which corruptions remain hard, limitations

stuck.label: I don't know how to structure the report
hints: Could a classmate repeat your experiment from the report alone? What would they still need to ask?
A short research report usually has a question, data and method, results with one main figure and one table, discussion, and limitations. The paper you started from follows a similar order.
Outline skeleton: 1. Question and why robustness matters, 2. Data (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-10-C), 3. Models and training, 4. Results, 5. Augmentation comparison, 6. Limitations.

stuck.label: I'm not sure my findings are general
hints: Would your conclusion still hold for larger images, other datasets or other network types?
Results from one small dataset and one architecture support careful conclusions about that setting only. Naming what you did not test is part of an honest report.
Sentence skeleton: 'For a small CNN on CIFAR-10, ___ caused the largest accuracy drop at severity 5, and training with ___ reduced the drop for ___ but not for ___.'

stuck.label: How do I connect my work to real-world AI?
hints: Where do cameras meet fog, blur or noise in everyday life, and why would a mistake there matter?
Robustness to ordinary corruptions matters for systems that use cameras outdoors or in poor light. Linking your results to such settings shows why the question is important, without overstating them.

Analogous example: a phone camera that fails in rain is annoying, while a car camera that fails in rain is dangerous. Pick one setting and explain what your results would and would not tell its designers.

quiz.question: An array x has shape (50000, 32, 32, 3). How many images does it hold?
quiz.explanation: The first dimension counts images; the others are height, width and color channels.

quiz.question: Which slice gives the third block of 10,000 images in x?
quiz.explanation: Blocks start at 0, 10,000 and 20,000, so the third block is x[20000:30000].

quiz.question: What is one epoch?
options: One full pass through the training data
quiz.explanation: An epoch means the model has seen every training example once.

quiz.question: Why move both the model and the batches to the GPU?
options: Computations need the model and data on the same device
quiz.explanation: PyTorch raises an error if tensors and model weights are on different devices.

quiz.concept: Accuracy and evaluation on a test set
quiz.question: Accuracy is:
options: The share of test images classified correctly
quiz.explanation: Correct predictions divided by all predictions.

quiz.concept: Accuracy and evaluation on a test set
quiz.question: Why must the corruption tests use the same saved model for every corruption?
options: So differences come from the corruptions, not from different models
quiz.explanation: Changing only one thing at a time is what makes the comparison fair.

quiz.question: What is distribution shift?
options: Test data that differs from the data the model was trained on
quiz.explanation: Corrupted images are a shift away from the clean training distribution.

quiz.question: What does data augmentation do during training?
options: Randomly changes training images so the model learns to ignore those changes
quiz.explanation: Augmented examples teach the model that certain changes should not affect the label.

guides.why: Images and labels are stored as numpy arrays.
guides.summary: numpy arrays hold many numbers in a grid with a shape. An image dataset is often one array whose first dimension counts images. Slicing selects parts of an array by position, which is how you pick one severity block or one image.
steps: Create arrays and read their shape
Load and save arrays with np.load and np.save
guides.practice: Make an array of shape (6, 4) with numbers 0 to 23 and slice out rows 2 to 3.

guides.why: You will train a small CNN on CIFAR-10.
guides.summary: A classifier learns from labeled images by adjusting its weights to reduce a loss. Training runs in epochs, each a pass over the data in small batches. A small convolutional network can learn CIFAR-10 in a short GPU session.
steps: Write a training loop with a loss and an optimizer
Track training and validation accuracy per epoch
guides.practice: Train any tiny network for two epochs and plot the loss after each batch.

guides.concept: Accuracy and evaluation on a test set
guides.why: You will compare accuracy on clean and corrupted test images.
guides.summary: Accuracy is the share of correct predictions. A model is evaluated on images it never trained on, and comparisons are fair only when everything except the factor being studied stays the same.
steps: Switch the model to evaluation mode
Predict on a test set without computing gradients
Compare models on identical test images
guides.practice: Compute accuracy by hand for ten predictions and their true labels.

guides.why: Corrupted images differ from training images; augmentation is one way to prepare a model for that.
guides.summary: Distribution shift happens when test data looks different from training data, such as blurred or noisy photos. Data augmentation randomly changes training images so the model becomes less sensitive to such changes, often with a small cost on clean images.
steps: See examples of common image corruptions
Apply torchvision transforms to training images
Compare clean and shifted accuracy before and after augmentation
guides.practice: Apply three different torchvision transforms to one image and show the results side by side.
